title: Joan of Arc (1412–1431)
hook: a farm girl who led armies, was burned at nineteen, and was declared innocent 25 years later

segments.voice: Yesterday, Catherine of Siena, who told a pope, lovingly, to come home. Your line was be who god meant. Did you say the one true thing? Day ninety.

Think about the most out-of-your-depth you've ever felt. A job you weren't qualified for. A room full of people who clearly thought you shouldn't be there. Now picture this. France, 1429, deep in a war with England that has dragged on for generations. A seventeen-year-old peasant girl from a village in the east, who can't read or write, walks into the court of the uncrowned king and tells him God has sent her to lift the siege of Orléans and see him crowned. The soldiers laugh. The advisers roll their eyes. And within a few months, she's done both. Today: Joan of Arc.
screen: `OUT OF YOUR DEPTH.` → `A FARM GIRL AT COURT.` → `ORLÉANS, 1429.`

segments.voice: Joan said that from about the age of thirteen she heard voices, which she identified as Saint Michael, Saint Catherine and Saint Margaret. They told her to go and help the king. She cut her hair, put on armor, and rode at the front of the army carrying a banner. She said at her trial that she loved her banner far more than her sword, and carried it so she wouldn't have to kill anyone. The siege of Orléans broke in about a week. That summer, the king was crowned at Reims with Joan standing beside him. Then it fell apart. A year later she was captured and sold to the English, who put her on trial before a church court run by a bishop on their side. She had no lawyer. For months, learned men tried to trap her. The most famous trap: are you in God's grace? Say yes, and she's proud. Say no, and she's condemned herself. A nineteen-year-old with no schooling answered, in effect: if I am not, may God put me there, and if I am, may God keep me there. The room went quiet. They burned her anyway, in Rouen, in 1431. She asked for a cross to be held up where she could see it. Twenty-five years later, with the pope's approval, a new church trial declared the first one unjust and cleared her name. In 1920 she was declared a saint. So the same Church that condemned her, through a bishop, later admitted it was wrong and honored her. And today's line? People often quote her as saying I am not afraid, I was born to do this. Nobody can find that sentence in the trial records. But the courage is all there.
screen: `VOICES, AND A BANNER.` · `ORLÉANS FREED, A KING CROWNED.` · `ARE YOU IN GOD'S GRACE?` · `CONDEMNED, THEN CLEARED.` · then, large: `IF I AM NOT, MAY GOD PUT ME THERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand by what you know is right. Settle and breathe. Think of one place in your life where you know what's right but you've been quiet: at work, in your family, in a group of friends. Feel where the fear sits in your body. Don't push it away. Joan was afraid too; she cried at her trial. Courage isn't no fear. It's fear that keeps walking. Picture one small step you could take. If you pray, you can ask for her courage. The bell holds the time.
Joan of Arc. A peasant girl who led armies, was burned at nineteen by a court that got it wrong, and was declared innocent twenty-five years later. Today's word.
Your line: I am not afraid. Today, take the one small step you pictured, even if your voice shakes. Day ninety.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Joan of Arc on 30 May; she is one of the patron saints of France, and many ask her prayers for courage.

trapdoor: what you thought: a French girl who fought the English and was burned as a witch.
what it means: a peasant girl who followed what she believed was God's call, was condemned by a partisan church court, and was later cleared and made a saint.
what a scholar hears: the trial records survive almost word for word. the final charge was relapsed heresy, not witchcraft, and the nullification came in 1456.

notes: All Joan material paraphrased from the trial records; the grace answer is given 'in effect' without quotation marks, since no approved public-domain translation was used.

The index carry 'I am not afraid' comes from a popular attribution ('I am not afraid... I was born to do this') not found in the trial records; the script says so. Keeper may want the index carry reconsidered.
Banner vs sword: trial session of 27 February 1431 ('forty times' more than her sword). Confirm.
Orléans siege lifted 8 May 1429 (Joan arrived 29 April); coronation at Reims 17 July 1429; captured at Compiègne May 1430; burned 30 May 1431 in Rouen. Confirm.
The tribunal was presided over by Bishop Pierre Cauchon, aligned with the English; the 1456 nullification was authorized by Pope Callixtus III. Confirm.
Canonized 16 May 1920 by Benedict XV. Confirm.
Final condemnation was for relapsed heresy (resuming male clothing), not witchcraft. Confirm.
'She cried at her trial' — accounts mention her weeping (e.g. at the threat of burning, and at Saint-Ouen). Confirm.
